title: County of Toulouse
capsule: The County of Toulouse was one of the most powerful principalities of southern France, ruled by the Raimundine dynasty from the late ninth century, dominating Languedoc and much of the Midi with ties to both the French crown and the Holy Roman Empire. Count Raymond IV led the First Crusade's Provençal contingent and briefly contested leadership of the crusading army, while his twelfth-century successors presided over a brilliant Occitan court culture centered on troubadour poetry. The county was devastated by the Albigensian Crusade launched in 1209 against Cathar heresy, and the Treaty of Paris (1229) forced Count Raymond VII to surrender half his lands and acknowledge French royal suzerainty; the county formally passed to the French crown in 1271 on the death of Joan of Toulouse, the last of the Raimundine line.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The county's core territories are well documented in medieval sources, but the precise extent of its fluctuating overlordship over sub-counties and viscounties is subject to scholarly debate.
